newsitem.title: ITALY: De Silguy says no plot to exclude anyone from EMU.
newsitem.headline: De Silguy says no plot to exclude anyone from EMU.

text.p: EU Commissioner Thibault de Silguy denied on Thursday there was a plot to exclude any country from joining a single European currency, adding that latecomers still had time to catch up before the euro hit the streets.
"All countries will be treated in the same way and the admission examination will be based on economic and not geographic criteria," De Silguy told a news conference.

Italy is in a race to restore order to its state finances by the end of 1997 and keep alive its chances of becoming a founding memeber of European economic and monetary union (EMU) when it takes off in 1999.
Analysts believe that Italy's entry into EMU may have to be delayed because of the weight of German public opinion against a eurocurrency which includes the lira from the start.

But in a speech delivered later on Thursday, de Silguy said that EU countries failing to qualify for EMU at the outset in 1999 could still clamber on board by the time the euro enters general use on January 1, 2002.
The euro is due to be used only for interbank transactions between 1999 and 2002.

"If it appears a state -- which was not included in the initial list of participants -- was able, taking into account its progress in (economic) reform, to rapidly respect the criteria, it could be possible, in my opinion, for it to introduce coins and notes at the same time as the others, that is to say on January 1, 2002," he said.

Some analysts believe this could be the basis of a face-saving formula which would allow Italy more time to clean up state finances while not being ruled out from adopting a single currency early next century.

"The date of January 1 1999 (for the EMU launch) will be respected for a number of reasons," said De Silguy. "There is a firm political determination of all the states, convergence is in progress and 1997 growth forecasts seem to me to be sufficient," he added.
De Silguy also said he believed a delay in launching EMU would be legally impossible and economically disastrous.

"It's juridically impossible because the Maastricht Treaty would have to be rewritten," he said. "Economically it would be suicide because there would be strong pressure for a slowdown in efforts (to qualify)."
It would give "an extremely negative message for the markets."
"All countries are making considerable efforts to reduce public deficits and I congratulate those finance ministers who have said they are ready to take further measures if necessary."
Italy is expected to ram through in the next few weeks a supplementary package of budgetary measures which will slice at least 14 trillion lire ($8.2 billion) off the public deficit.
The government is going all out to slash the deficit-to- gross domestic product (GDP) ratio -- a key target under the Maastricht criteria -- to three percent by end-1997.
De Silguy said the European Union was on course to achieve 1997 growth of 2.3 percent, although Italy was growing more slowly.
"On the basis of today's data I confirm the forecasts made in the autumn of 2.3 percent annual growth in Europe for 1997 compared to 1.6 percent in 1996," he said.

"The Italian data are slightly lower," he said. "Even on the basis of surveys, the confidence of investors is returning," he added. The EU Commission is forecasting 1.4 percent growth for Italy in 1997. ($ = 1705 Italian Lire)
